title: Presumed cytomegalovirus retinitis as the initial infectious manifestation of previously unrecognized Good syndrome in an HIV-negative patient: a case report.
authors: Yang C, Xiong J, Huang J et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis is a sight-threatening opportunistic infection that is uncommon in HIV-negative individuals without identifiable secondary cause of immunosuppression. Good syndrome (GS) is a rare adult-onset immunodeficiency associated with thymoma, and CMV retinitis as its initial infectious presentation is exceptionally rare.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 47-year-old HIV-negative woman presented with blurred vision in the right eye for 1 month. She had a history of thymectomy for type AB thymoma and left-eye pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) 2 years earlier. At presentation, best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was light perception (LP) in the right eye and no light perception (NLP) in the left eye. Fundus examination revealed extensive hemorrhagic necrotizing retinitis involving the posterior pole and macula. B-scan ultrasonography showed dense vitreous opacities and localized retinal detachment. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed retinal thickening, hyperreflective lesions, and disruption of the retinal architecture. The markedly elevated serum CMV DNA level, together with the characteristic fundus findings, supported a clinical diagnosis of presumed CMV retinitis. Intraocular polymerase chain reaction (PCR) confirmation was unavailable because the patient declined aqueous humor sampling. Immunologic evaluation demonstrated absence of peripheral CD19+ B cells, hypogammaglobulinemia, reduced CD4+ T-cell count, and an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio. In the setting of prior thymoma, these findings supported the diagnosis of GS. The patient was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and intravenous ganciclovir. Serum CMV DNA levels declined substantially after treatment, but visual recovery was limited.
CONCLUSIONS: Presumed CMV retinitis may be the initial infectious manifestation of previously unrecognized GS, with typical combined humoral and cellular immunodeficiency already evident at presentation. In HIV-negative patients with presumed CMV retinitis and no evident secondary immunosuppression, underlying immunodeficiency should be actively investigated. Particular attention should be paid to a history of thymoma, and early systemic immunologic evaluation should be considered to reduce diagnostic delay and irreversible visual loss.

title: Recent advances in the treatment of pleural mesothelioma.
authors: Jakopović M, Ljubičić L, Bitar L
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: In a short period, pleural mesothelioma has undergone major revisions in its nomenclature, grading, staging, and treatment approach. In this review, we provide an updated overview of recent advances in diagnosing, biomarker research, and treating malignant pleural mesothelioma.
RECENT FINDINGS: Five-year follow-up from CheckMate 743 confirms a durable survival benefit with nivolumab plus ipilimumab (hazard ratio 0.74), greater in nonepithelioid disease (hazard ratio 0.48) than in epithelioid disease (hazard ratio 0.85). BEAT-meso, evaluating atezolizumab added to bevacizumab-chemotherapy, missed its primary overall survival (OS) endpoint overall, but the same histology-dependent pattern recurred: a clear benefit in nonepithelioid disease (17.9 vs. 10 months; hazard ratio 0.51) and none in epithelioid disease (hazard ratio 1.00). Adding pembrolizumab to platinum-pemetrexed improved OS overall survival (hazard ratio 0.79), especially in nonepithelioid disease, leading to FDA approval regardless of histology. Pegargiminase became the first metabolically targeted agent to improve survival in nonepithelioid mesothelioma. MARS 2 showed that pleurectomy decortication added to chemotherapy shortens survival and worsens quality of life. Hemithoracic IMRT after pleurectomy/decortication showed consistent survival benefit across cohorts.
SUMMARY: First-line treatment is now determined by histology and the patient's performance status rather than by any molecular biomarker. The main unmet needs remain epithelioid disease, second-line therapy, and a validated predictive biomarker.

title: Intrathyroidal thymic carcinoma with delayed cervical lymph node metastasis 5 years postoperatively: a case report with focus on ultrasonic features.
authors: Ren Y, Qin X, Zhang H et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intrathyroidal thymic carcinoma (ITTC) is a rare thyroid malignancy with nonspecific imaging features. The ultrasonographic characteristics of its metastatic lymph nodes, particularly in cases of delayed metastasis, remain poorly understood.
OBJECTIVE: To report a case of ITTC with cervical lymph node metastasis occurring 5 years after surgery, with a focus on the ultrasonographic features of both the primary and metastatic lesions.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 32-year-old woman presented with hoarseness and choking. Ultrasound revealed a solid, hypoechoic mass in the lower pole of the left thyroid lobe. The lesion exhibited ill-defined margins, an irregular shape, heterogeneous echogenicity with short linear hyperechoic internal strands and predominantly peripheral vascularity on colour Doppler flow imaging (CDFI). Total thyroidectomy with lymph node dissection was performed, and histopathology confirmed ITTC. During the 5-year follow-up period, surveillance ultrasound detected an abnormal lymph node in the left level IV of the neck. This node showed well-defined borders, loss of corticomedullary differentiation, an absent hilum and no significant vascularity on CDFI. Fine-needle aspiration cytology and subsequent surgical pathology confirmed metastasis from ITTC.
CONCLUSIONS: The characteristic ultrasonographic features of primary ITTC lesions include a solid hypoechoic mass in the mid-to-lower pole of the thyroid, with ill-defined margins, an irregular shape, internal short linear hyperechoic strands and typically peripheral vascularity, often without calcification or cystic change. Metastatic lymph nodes may demonstrate well-defined borders, loss of corticomedullary differentiation, an absent hilum and scant vascularity. Recognition of these ultrasonographic patterns is crucial for the early identification, accurate diagnosis and long-term management of ITTC.

title: Targeting the CCL5-CCR5 axis protects against chemoresistant mesothelioma development through macrophage reprogramming.
authors: Gerardelli L, Havrics E, Demanche A et al.
abstract: Treatment resistance in pleural mesothelioma (PM) is a clinical challenge. Cisplatin-based chemotherapy remains a cornerstone of treatment, but responses are transient as resistant tumor cells drive disease progression. The contribution of the tumor immune microenvironment to chemoresistance is poorly understood so far. Using cisplatin-resistant murine (AB12, PM27) and human (MSTO-211H) PM models combined with transcriptomics, immune profiling and functional assays, we identify a key role for the CCL5-CCR5 axis in shaping an immunosuppressive niche that supports tumor progression. Resistant cells upregulate and secrete high levels of CCL5, leading to enhanced tumor growth in vivo. Immune profiling of tumor microenvironment reveals a marked recruitment of CCR5+ macrophages displaying an immunosuppressive phenotype characterized by reduced inflammatory activity. Mechanistically, tumor-derived CCL5 promotes macrophage recruitment and polarization toward a pro-tumoral state through CCR5 signaling. Disruption of this axis, either by pharmacological inhibition of CCR5 using maraviroc or by genetic silencing of CCL5, reduces macrophage infiltration and significantly impairs tumor progression. These findings reveal microenvironment-driven mechanism of chemoresistance in PM and identify the CCL5-CCR5 axis as a key vulnerability. Targeting this pathway may therefore represent a promising therapeutic strategy to limit the progression of cisplatin-resistant mesothelioma by disrupting the tumor-supportive immune microenvironment.
